title: Parallelization
summary: Run several model calls at the same time and combine the results. Sectioning splits a task into independent parts. Voting repeats one task to get diverse answers.
useIf: Subtasks are independent, or you want several independent attempts at the same question, and cost and rate limits allow the extra calls.
avoidIf: Branches need each other's output, share state they could corrupt, or you have no rule for combining conflicting results.

explain.md: Anthropic describes two variations of **parallelization** [[r1]]. In **sectioning** you break a task into independent subtasks that run at once, for example screening a request for policy problems in one call while another call answers it. In **voting** you run the same task several times and combine the outputs, for example several reviewers checking code for vulnerabilities. Microsoft's concurrent orchestration is the same fan-out and fan-in shape, also called scatter-gather or map-reduce, and its documentation lists brainstorming, ensemble reasoning and quorum voting as fits [[r9]][[tr2]].

explain.title: Fan-out and fan-in
explain.alt: One input fans out to three parallel branches. An aggregator merges their results into one output.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  I[Input] --> A[Branch A]
  I --> B[Branch B]
  I --> C[Branch C]
  A --> G[Aggregate]
  B --> G
  C --> G
  G --> O[Output]

explain.title: Latency and cost of a fan-out
explain.expr: latency = max(branch_latency) + aggregate_latency     cost = sum(branch_cost) + aggregate_cost

vars.v: code or an LLM call that merges, votes or ranks the branch outputs

explain.example: Branches of 4 s, 6 s and 5 s plus a 2 s merge take **8 s**, against 17 s in sequence. The token bill is still the sum of all three.

explain.md: Voting has a research root: self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and takes the most consistent answer, and the paper reports gains such as +17.9 percent on GSM8K over greedy chain-of-thought [[tr5]]. The catch is that you pay for every vote, and votes from the same model share its blind spots. Sectioning needs a clean boundary: if two branches edit the same artifact or touch the same external system, they need a conflict rule, or they should not run in parallel [[r9]].

explain.title: Check quota before you fan out
explain.md: Parallel branches hit tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute limits together. Cap concurrency and handle throttling (HTTP 429) with backoff, or the speed gain turns into retries.

whereToUse: Running a guardrail check alongside the main answer call
Summarising or classifying many independent documents or sections
Multi-perspective review, such as security, cost and readability reviewers
Voting on high-stakes classifications where a single call is unreliable
Prefetching several retrieval sources at once

use: Branches do not depend on each other
Wall-clock time matters and quota allows the concurrency
A clear aggregation rule exists: merge, majority vote, ranking or a judge
avoid: Agents must build on each other's work in sequence
Branches write to shared state without a conflict strategy
Quota or cost makes parallel calls infeasible
Aggregation logic is so complex that it lowers quality [[r9]]
flips: Subtasks turn out to depend on each other: switch to a chain
Votes agree almost always: cut the voters, you are paying for no information
The split cannot be known in advance: move to orchestrator-workers

pitfalls.symptom: Bursts of 429 errors and slower-than-sequential runs
pitfalls.cause: Fan-out exceeded rate limits and every branch retried
pitfalls.fix: Cap concurrency, add jitter to retries and queue branches.

pitfalls.cause: Branches made conflicting decisions with no rule for resolving them
pitfalls.fix: Define precedence or a tie-break, or serialise the branches that touch the same thing.

pitfalls.symptom: Voting adds cost but no accuracy
pitfalls.cause: Voters are the same model with the same prompt, so errors are correlated
pitfalls.fix: Vary prompts, models or evidence, and measure whether votes ever disagree.

scenarios.title: Many independent sections
scenarios.situation: A job reads a 60-section document and must produce a short finding for each section, then one combined report. Sections do not reference each other. The model quota allows about 20 concurrent calls.
constraints: Report merge is a final step
unknowns: Do findings need a shared glossary or style?
scenarios.question: How do you run it?

options.name: Sectioning with concurrency capped at the quota, then one merge call
options.why: Independent parts parallelise cleanly and the cap avoids self-inflicted throttling.
options.tradeoff: Total tokens equal sequential processing, and style can drift across sections unless the prompt pins it.

options.name: Sequential chain over all 60 sections
options.why: Simple, steady and consistent in style.
options.tradeoff: Latency is about 60 calls long for no dependency reason.

options.name: Fire all 60 calls at once
options.why: It overruns the quota and triggers throttling and retries.
options.tradeoff: Fine only when quota comfortably exceeds the fan-out, for instance in a batch tier.

flips.then: A batch API or queue can lower cost, at the price of latency.
Chain the dependent sections and parallelise the rest.

scenarios.takeaway: Parallelise what is independent, and size the fan-out to your quota.

scenarios.title: Voting on a risky label
scenarios.situation: A classifier decides whether a message needs human review. A missed case is costly, and the single-call model is right about 90 percent of the time.
constraints: Cost of a miss is high
Latency of two seconds is acceptable
unknowns: Do the votes disagree on the hard cases or all fail together?
Is a human review queue available for disagreements?
scenarios.question: Do you add voting?

options.name: Three diverse votes with a human queue for disagreements
options.why: Disagreement is a useful signal, and diversity in prompts or models reduces correlated errors.
options.tradeoff: Triple the classification cost and added review work.

options.name: Run the same prompt five times at temperature zero
options.why: Near-identical outputs add cost without new information.
options.tradeoff: Sampling at higher temperature is closer to self-consistency, but still shares the model's blind spots.

options.name: Keep one call and tighten the prompt
options.why: Cheapest, and prompt fixes may close part of the gap.
options.tradeoff: No signal on uncertain cases, so misses stay silent.

flips.if: Votes never disagree on a labelled sample
flips.then: Drop to one call and spend the budget elsewhere.
Vote only when a cheap first call is low confidence.

scenarios.takeaway: Votes are worth paying for only when they can disagree for informative reasons.

quiz.q: Three branches take 4 s, 6 s and 5 s and run in parallel. Merging takes 2 s. How many seconds does the fan-out take end to end?
quiz.hint: Parallel time is the slowest branch plus the merge.
quiz.explain: max(4, 6, 5) + 2 = 8 s. Sequential would be 4 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 17 s. The token cost is the sum of all branches either way.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason NOT to parallelise two agents?
options: Each takes more than a second
Both write to the same document with no conflict rule
Their outputs are in different formats
quiz.explain: Concurrent writes to shared state without a conflict strategy are named in Microsoft's list of cases to avoid. Different prompts, durations and formats are normal in parallel branches. [[r9]]

quiz.q: What is the difference between sectioning and voting?
options: Sectioning runs different independent subtasks, voting runs the same task several times
Sectioning is sequential, voting is parallel
Sectioning needs a judge model, voting does not
They are the same pattern with different names
quiz.explain: Sectioning divides work into independent parts, while voting repeats the same task for diverse outputs. Both are parallel, and either may use code or a model to aggregate. [[r1]]

flashcards.front: Name the two variations of parallelization.
flashcards.back: Sectioning (independent subtasks at once) and voting (the same task run several times for diverse outputs) [[r1]].
max(branch latency) plus the aggregation step. Cost is the sum of all branches plus aggregation.

flashcards.front: Why might voting add cost but no accuracy?
flashcards.back: Votes from the same model and prompt share blind spots, so errors correlate. Diversify prompts, models or evidence and check that votes ever disagree.
